purpose: Natamycin is used to treat fungal infections of the eye, such as infections of the cornea (the clear front part of your eye), eyelids, and the tissue around the eye. It is most commonly used for a condition called fungal keratitis, which is a fungal infection of the cornea. Your doctor may prescribe it after an eye injury or if you wear contact lenses and develop an infection.
how_it_works: Natamycin works by attacking the outer wall (called the cell membrane) of fungal cells and making holes in it. This causes the fungus to lose important substances it needs to survive, which kills it. Think of it like poking holes in a balloon — the fungus simply cannot hold itself together and dies off.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects happen in or around the eye and include eye irritation, burning or stinging when you apply the drops, blurred vision right after using the drops, redness of the eye, and sensitivity to light. These effects are usually mild and temporary.
warnings: Do not wear contact lenses while using this medication unless your doctor specifically tells you it is okay. Tell your doctor if your eye gets worse instead of better, or if you develop swelling, increased pain, or discharge. Do not share this medication with anyone else. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, check with your doctor before using it. Keep the bottle clean and avoid touching the dropper tip to your eye or any surface to prevent contamination.
typical_dosing: The usual dose for eye infections is 1 drop placed into the affected eye every 1 to 2 hours during the first few days, then reduced to 1 drop every 3 to 4 hours as the infection improves. Treatment usually lasts 2 to 3 weeks or as directed by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as dosing can vary depending on how serious your infection is.
